summary: In the present tense Hebrew has no verb “to be”: the subject and what it is simply stand side by side — אֲנִי סְטוּדֶנְט “I (am) a student”, הַמּוֹרֶה פֹּה “the teacher (is) here”. This is a nominal sentence. In the past and future the verb הָיָה appears and agrees with the subject: הוּא הָיָה מוֹרֶה “he was a teacher”, הִיא הָיְתָה סְטוּדֶנְטִית, הֵם הָיוּ חֲבֵרִים; הוּא יִהְיֶה / הִיא תִּהְיֶה “he / she will be”. Between two nouns, especially in definitions, a pronoun that agrees with the subject can stand where “is” would be: יֶלֶד הוּא אָדָם “a child is a person”.

items.title: Present — no verb
points: אֲנִי סְטוּדֶנְט — I am a student
הִיא מוֹרָה — she is a teacher
הַסֵּפֶר פֹּה — the book is here
זֶה בַּיִת — this is a house

items.title: Past and future — הָיָה
points: אֲנִי הָיִיתִי סְטוּדֶנְט — I was a student
הִיא הָיְתָה מוֹרָה — she was a teacher
הַסֵּפֶר הָיָה פֹּה — the book was here
הִיא תִּהְיֶה מוֹרָה — she will be a teacher

head: past
future
blocks.caption: The forms of הָיָה you meet now (the rest of the future comes with the verb lessons). Everyday spelling of הָיְתָה: הייתה.

blocks.text: Word order stays the same as in English: subject first, then the predicate. In the past the verb goes between them: הַמּוֹרָה הָיְתָה פֹּה.

blocks.title: Agreement in the past
blocks.text: הָיָה agrees with the subject, not with the noun after it: הַמִּטָּה הָיְתָה שָׁם (מִטָּה is feminine), הַשֻּׁלְחָן הָיָה פֹּה, הַסְּפָרִים הָיוּ פֹּה.

blocks.title: Do not invent a present
blocks.text: There is no *אֲנִי הוֹוֶה סְטוּדֶנְט and no *אֲנִי הָיָה סְטוּדֶנְט for “I am”. הָיָה is always past: “was”.

blocks.title: Russian already does this
blocks.text: Я студент — Он был учителем — Она была студенткой: no verb in the present, a gendered verb in the past. Hebrew works the same way: אֲנִי סְטוּדֶנְט — הוּא הָיָה מוֹרֶה — הִיא הָיְתָה סְטוּדֶנְטִית.

blocks.title: The pronoun as “is”
blocks.text: With a noun subject, especially in definitions, Hebrew can put הוּא / הִיא / הֵם / הֵן where English has “is / are”: יֶלֶד הוּא אָדָם, יְלָדִים הֵם אֲנָשִׁים. It agrees with the subject. With a pronoun subject it is not used: אֲנִי מוֹרֶה, never *אֲנִי הוּא מוֹרֶה.

blocks.title: Ask yourself
questions: Was it, or will it be? → a form of הָיָה.
Who or what is the subject: masculine, feminine, plural?

askYourself: Is the sentence about now? → no verb at all: subject + noun / place.
Is it about the past? → הָיָה in the form of the subject: הָיִיתִי, הָיָה, הָיְתָה, הָיוּ …
Is it about the future? → יִהְיֶה (he), תִּהְיֶה (she), אֶהְיֶה (I) …
What is the gender and number of the subject? The verb follows the subject, not the noun after it.
Is the subject a noun and the predicate a noun, as in a definition? → you may add הוּא / הִיא / הֵם / הֵן (agreeing with the subject).
Is it “there is / there are”? → that is יֵשׁ (lesson 6), not a form of הָיָה in the present.
steps: Decide the time: present, past or future.
Present: put the subject and the predicate side by side.
Past or future: insert the form of הָיָה that agrees with the subject.

traps: No present “to be”: אֲנִי מוֹרֶה, not *אֲנִי הוּא מוֹרֶה or *אֲנִי הָיָה מוֹרֶה.
Past agreement follows the subject: הַדֶּלֶת הָיְתָה שָׁם (feminine), not *הַדֶּלֶת הָיָה שָׁם.
In the past the pronoun can be dropped (הָיִיתִי סְטוּדֶנְט), in the present it cannot (אֲנִי סְטוּדֶנְט).
The pronoun copula agrees with the subject, not with the predicate: אִשָּׁה הִיא אָדָם (אִשָּׁה is feminine, although אָדָם is masculine).

seeAlso.note: Arabic too has a verbless present (أَنَا طَالِبٌ “I (am) a student”) and uses كَانَ in the past — which, unlike Hebrew הָיָה, puts the predicate in the accusative.
German always says the verb and conjugates it for person: ich bin, du bist, er ist — Hebrew says nothing in the present.
Chinese 是 links two nouns (我是学生) but is not used before adjectives (他很高); Hebrew needs no linking word for either.
